title: Department of War Daily Briefing
description: Secretary-level initiatives, acquisition, Golden Dome, operations and policy across the Department of War.
readFirst: Covers Nov. 16–25. New: Bloomberg Government reported Nov. 24 that Secretary Pete Hegseth is rejecting Senate language that would require commanders to keep ultimate human responsibility over lethal force by autonomous weapons and artificial intelligence. The White House request for a $5 billion Golden Dome anomaly in the next continuing resolution is on the budget page. No new Golden Dome program release dated Nov. 24–25 was opened on war.gov. No new Department of War enterprise software agreement in that window was found. war.gov posted contracts for Nov. 24 and no news releases; no Nov. 25 contract list was posted at the time of this edition.

items.headline: Hegseth rejects Senate language on human responsibility for AI weapons
items.summary: Bloomberg Government reported Nov. 24 that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is rejecting a Senate defense-policy proposal that would require the military's autonomous weapons and artificial intelligence to be designed and deployed so commanders exercise "ultimate human responsibility" over the use of lethal force. Bloomberg Government said the Senate Armed Services Committee put the language in its version of the annual defense authorization bill as lawmakers sought, for the first time, to regulate the military's use of artificial intelligence and autonomous technology. The report said those proposals come as the Pentagon seeks to accelerate artificial-intelligence adoption on the battlefield and as technology executives sell advanced AI tools to the department.

items.headline: Clayton will act as national cyber director while Davies awaits confirmation
items.summary: Axios reported Nov. 23 that Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton will serve as acting national cyber director while Kirsten Davies, the Pentagon's chief information officer, awaits Senate confirmation, and that a White House official said President Trump nominated her to lead the office permanently rather than leave her in an acting role. Axios said Davies will assist Clayton as a senior adviser until she is confirmed, and that Trump announced Thursday he was tapping her to replace Sean Cairncross. The White House said Nov. 20 that Trump had named Davies the day before. Federal News Network reported Nov. 20 that Davies became department CIO last December and that the department had not yet said who will replace her.

items.headline: War Department adopts ACME to classify and declassify records with super intelligence
items.summary: The Department of War reported Nov. 23 that the Automated Classification Management Environment is meant to use super intelligence and automated workflows to classify and declassify records. Paola Apodaca, chief of declassification for the undersecretary of war for intelligence and security, said the system will speed classification for documents from the department's more than 5 million service members, civilians, and contractors. The department said records management costs taxpayers more than $15 billion a year, and that users now manually search more than 4,000 security classification guides. It said Deputy Secretary Steve Feinberg adopted ACME as an enterprise solution in October, appointed Air Force Secretary Troy Meink to oversee it, and that the tools grew out of a $2.35 million investment by Under Secretary Bradley Hansell and Cameron Stanley, the department's chief super intelligence officer.

items.headline: War Department asks states to propose a Next Great American Base
items.summary: The Department of War reported Nov. 17 that it released a video asking state and local officials to propose locations, before a December deadline, for a prototype all-domain installation it calls the Next Great American Base. Assistant Secretary Dale Marks, for energy, infrastructure and environment, said the department is not building an installation for today's doctrine and wants a platform for 2050 and beyond, including layered defenses against hypersonic strikes, directed energy, cyber intrusions, orbital surveillance, and electromagnetic warfare. Marks said the base should sustain power, water, data, and defense off the civilian grid for up to 90 consecutive days, and that strategic facilities may need to sit hundreds of feet underground.

items.headline: DISA asks industry for a cloud identity service at IL5 and IL6
items.summary: Federal News Network reported Nov. 19 that the Defense Information Systems Agency posted an other-transaction agreement on SAM.gov on Nov. 9 for a modular, cloud-hosted commercial identity service operating at Impact Levels 5 and 6. The notice says the prototype must cover a federated identity provider, automated account provisioning, a master entitlement record, and a federation hub, and Federal News Network said white papers are due Nov. 30. Brian Hermann, director of the portfolio acquisition executive for cyber at DISA, told Federal News Network he wants a demonstration in about six months and then a fast cutover off the legacy system, which he said relies on more than 300 on-premise authentication servers. Hermann said a later agreement would cover regional and tactical disconnected identity, which he described as a different problem from the enterprise service.

items.headline: War Department advances software to command mixed unmanned fleets
items.summary: The Department of War said Nov. 19 that it advanced the Autonomous Vehicle Orchestrator, software meant to let one operator command a mixed fleet of unmanned vehicles across domains. The department said the AVO Challenge, launched Jan. 13, 2026, evaluated scalable, vehicle-agnostic tools and included live testing, and that results will be made public when the challenge is finished. Senior Chief Petty Officer Max Strasiser, a Navy SEAL serving as chief operating officer for Project Agincourt and the direct reporting program manager for unmanned systems, said Maj. Zach Laser and his team are leading the move from standalone platforms to a coordinated force. The department said the effort supports fielding low-cost, consumable drones and that vehicles alone do not provide that advantage.

items.headline: Seven laser teams are invited to a mid-December counter-drone shoot-off at Dugway
items.summary: The Department of War said Nov. 16 that its Office of Research and Engineering and Joint Interagency Task Force 401 invited seven industry teams, chosen from 13 white papers, to Phase II of a directed-energy counter-drone evaluation, with live fire at Dugway Proving Ground planned for mid-December. The systems are Allen Control Systems' Bullfrog, Aurelius Systems' Archimedes, AeroVironment (BlueHalo) Locust X1, Kord Technologies' Firefly, Lockheed Martin (IPG) Crossbow, Thor Dynamics' Laser Armor, and Yrikka's Talos drone-based laser. Brig. Gen. Matthew Ross, director of the task force, said the shoot-off is structured so a system that performs successfully can immediately result in a purchase order. Under Secretary Emil Michael said scaled directed energy is one of the department's six critical technology areas.

items.headline: Golden Dome deputy says the continuing resolution is not slowing execution
items.summary: DefenseScoop reported Nov. 19 that Marcia Holmes, deputy director for Golden Dome for America, said at the Evercore National Defense Forum that the program is not concerned about the continuing resolution because Congress provided a lot of fiscal 2026 money and the program is on contract and executing. DefenseScoop said that funding is nearly $25 billion from last year's reconciliation law, which Holmes called colorless money the department can spend over multiple years, and that Holmes said 100 percent of the program's funding is obligated. A Pentagon official told DefenseScoop the goal is initial operational capability by the summer of 2028, with the layered system finished in 2035. DefenseScoop said the department requested $398 million in discretionary funds and $17.1 billion in one-time mandatory spending this year, and that Senate appropriators would add another $9.4 billion in fiscal 2027 on top of the near-$400 million base appropriation.

items.headline: Hegseth memo would limit some Canada defense contacts; Ottawa sees no operational change
items.summary: CBC News reported Nov. 21 that the Washington Post said Secretary Pete Hegseth circulated a classified memo last week restricting U.S.-Canada military cooperation, and that Canadian defence officials said Saturday they had seen no change at the operational level. Sen. Mike Rounds told CBC the memo limits general and flag officer meetings to those that advance Department of War objectives and requires permission before officials attend social events or think-tank conferences, and that the measures were drafted months ago and signed recently. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told CBC the guidance does not affect defense intelligence cooperation, NORAD, or NATO. Defence Minister David McGuinty told CBC he first heard of the directive the day before and that the countries continue to work together on Caribbean drug interdiction and integrated air and missile defence.

items.headline: Hegseth delivers a C-130 to Colombia and $13.5 million in equipment to Honduras
items.summary: The Department of War reported Nov. 20 that after his Nov. 18 visit to Venezuela, Secretary Pete Hegseth traveled to Colombia, Ecuador, and Honduras. In Bogota he delivered a C-130 Hercules to Colombia's air force. In Quito he met President Daniel Noboa and told personnel at the U.S. embassy that Ecuador is a founding member of the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition, which the department said was established in March and has 19 countries. In Comayagua he visited Joint Task Force Bravo and delivered a $13.5 million down payment in military combat equipment. The department said this was his third trip to Central and South America since he was sworn in.

items.headline: Hegseth announces a U.S.-Venezuela military cooperation agreement in Caracas
items.summary: The Spokesman-Review, carrying a Reuters report, said Nov. 18 that Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a military cooperation agreement with Venezuela in Caracas covering joint training, intelligence sharing, and other cooperation, his first visit since U.S. forces deposed President Nicolas Maduro in a January raid. The Department of War reported Nov. 19 that Hegseth, speaking outside the U.S. Embassy on Nov. 18, said he was the first secretary of war to visit in more than a century and that the department will work with Venezuela through the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition. Al Jazeera reported Nov. 19 that the agreement also covers military equipment and border security, that Hegseth met Defence Minister Gustavo Gonzalez Lopez, and that the full terms have not been made public.

items.headline: Colby tells allies to fund Ukraine's front line, not deep strikes on cities
items.summary: The Department of War published Nov. 17 remarks by Under Secretary for Policy Elbridge Colby to the Ukraine Defense Contact Group. Colby said that in October, for the second consecutive month, Ukraine gained more territory than Russia, and that Russian forces suffered their highest monthly casualty toll of the war. He said support should focus on the front line and mid-range strikes, and that deep strikes on civilian infrastructure such as Wildberries have probably hardened Russian resolve. He said Ukraine will need continued funding for the PURL initiative, that this responsibility will rest primarily on Europe, and that the United States will keep facilitating high-end procurement through JUMPSTART, including what he called the first partner-funded procurement of Patriot interceptors for Ukraine.
